newsitem.title: GERMANY: Protesters jeer as nuclear waste arrives at dump.
newsitem.headline: Protesters jeer as nuclear waste arrives at dump.

text.p: A controversial nuclear waste shipment arrived by road at a dump in northern Germany on Wednesday, completing the last leg of a journey that thousands of anti-nuclear activists had tried to stop.

As the convoy of flatbed trucks carrying six containers of spent fuel rods rolled through the gates of Gorleben storage depot under a heavy escort of police backed by water cannon, protesters raised a chorus of boos and whistles, and chanted: "Get out".

What should have been a relatively short, simple journey from a loading station in Dannenberg, 20 km (16 miles) away, took three hours to complete as about 5,000 demonstrators along roads leading to the dump did their best to block the way.
Some of the trucks's windscreens were hit by paint bombs and it was all but impossible to see in or out of them.

Environmentalists accused the authorities of brutality in suppressing the demonstration, saying the protests were an expression of popular dissent. But the Bonn government condemned the protesters for "abusing the right to demonstrate" and said it would not change its energy policy.

It took Germany's biggest and most costly post-World War Two security operation, involving 30,000 police nationwide, to ensure the radioactive shipment from two German power stations and a French reprocessing plant arrived safely at the dump.
Each phase of its three-day journey was hindered by protesters pressing demands for a nuclear-free Germany.
Border guards in helicopters hovered over the area, which looked as though it had been hit by civil war.
The whole operation was expected to cost at least 66 million marks ($39 million) and surpass the 46 million marks spent on bringing a smaller shipment to Gorleben last year.
The waste was transported by train from the southern town of Walheim early on Monday and unloaded on to flat-bed trucks in the northern town of Dannenberg on Tuesday.

About 4,000 protesters staged sit-down protests to blockade the entrance of the loading station there and thousands of riot police removed each one individually before turning water cannon on them to clear them away.

Along the route from there to Gorleben, police said masked militants fired flare pistols, lobbed petrol bombs and pelted riot police with stones. Police said "anarchists" also set a police car on fire.

Environmental groups accused security forces of brutality saying about 150 people had been injured and that two of them had to be flown to hospital by helicopter. But officials argued police tactics were justified to protect the shipment.

"Setting water cannon in sub-zero temperatures on thousands of peaceful anti-nuclear protesters is an abuse of state power," said Pico Jordan, leader of the Greens party in Lower Saxony state's regional assembly.
But Interior Minister Manfred Kanther told Reuters Television in Nuremberg only police on the spot could decide the most appropriate tactics and condemned attacks on police.
"A law-abiding state does not want violence and does not provoke it either, but it does not allow itself to be held to ransom by violent perpetrators," Kanther said.

"Those who protest against nuclear waste transportation must admit they are supporting people who dig under roads, set trip-wires in the woods to injure police or shoot petrol bombs at helicopters," Kanther said.

German government spokesman Peter Hausmann said some protesters had abused the freedom to demonstrate and that Bonn would stand firm despite the protests because it saw no reason to its policy of using nuclear power as a source of energy.

But opposition Social Democrats said in a statement its leaders were willing to talk to members of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling coalition government about alternatives to transporting nuclear waste across the country.
"These transportations can be avoided. Time is running out for the government," it said.
